title: Latent heat of vaporisation
log: 2026-11-01T08:04:32Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new
2026-11-01T08:14:03Z write: the API refused it in the chapter request, so it is written on its own next

match.reason: The bank point teaches calorimetry, measuring heat from temperature change with q = mcΔT, while the new point is about the energy needed for water to evaporate (latent heat of vaporisation), which is a different idea.

draft.title: Latent heat of vaporisation
card: Latent heat of vaporisation is the energy needed to change a liquid into a gas at its boiling point or during evaporation, with no change in temperature. The energy is used to separate particles, not to speed them up.
Water has a high latent heat of vaporisation. Many hydrogen bonds between water molecules must be broken before a molecule can escape as vapour.
When water evaporates from a surface, the energy it takes comes from what is left behind. The remaining water and the surface cool down.
This is why sweating cools the body, and why evaporation from oceans and lakes helps limit how much their temperatures rise.
draft.remember: Evaporating water absorbs a lot of energy, so evaporation cools the surface it leaves.

a.q: Why does a large amount of energy need to be absorbed for liquid water to evaporate?
opts: Hydrogen bonds between molecules must be broken
Covalent bonds inside each molecule must be broken
The water must first be cooled to a lower temperature
The molecules must be made to move more slowly
a.why: Molecules can only escape as vapour once the hydrogen bonds holding them to their neighbours are broken, and this takes a lot of energy. The covalent bonds inside each molecule stay intact, so that option is wrong.
a.clue: Think about what holds one water molecule to the next.

b.q: Layla steps out of a pool on a warm day and feels cold as the water on her skin dries. What best explains this?
opts: Evaporating water takes energy from her skin
Evaporating water gives energy to her skin
Water on her skin is colder than the air
Her skin loses energy by breaking covalent bonds
b.why: Water needs a lot of energy to evaporate, and this energy comes from her skin, so her skin cools. The water gaining energy is true, but it takes that energy from her skin rather than giving it to her.
b.clue: Where does the energy for evaporation come from?

a.best: Hydrogen bonds between molecules must be broken

b.best: Evaporating water takes energy from her skin
